dominicalIntent: The opening of Exodus presents a Christological typology in the very names of Israel's sons, whose descent into Egypt prefigures the Incarnation—Christ, the true Israel, descending into the world of sin and death to redeem it. The seventy souls echo the seventy nations of Genesis 10, indicating that this 'holy nation' (Exodus 19:6) will be the instrument through which all nations are blessed, fulfilled in the Great Commission and the ingathering of the Gentiles into the New Israel, the Church.
cccReferences: CCC 62 (the patriarchs' descendants prefigure Christ's people); CCC 2574 (Israel as God's firstborn son, a type of Christ the true firstborn); CCC 2816 (the New Israel as the Church fulfilling the promise to Abraham through the twelve apostles).
historicalContext: The transition from Genesis to Exodus reflects genuine Egyptian historical realities of the Second Intermediate Period (c. 1650–1550 BCE), when Semitic-speaking peoples, particularly the Hyksos ('rulers of foreign lands'), established dynastic rule in Lower Egypt. The Delta region of Goshen (Wadi Tumilat) was precisely the frontier zone where Semitic pastoralists were permitted to graze their flocks, as confirmed by the Papyrus Anastasi VI describing Shasu-bedouin in the eastern Delta. The figure of 'seventy souls' corresponds to administrative census practices in both Egyptian and Mesopotamian contexts, where tribal units were enumerated for labor and taxation purposes.
translationNuances: Hebrew: שְׁמוֹת (shemot, 'names')—the Hebrew title of the book derives from the first significant word, following ancient Near Eastern titular convention. The LXX title Ἔξοδος ('Exodus,' 'going out') reflects theological interpretation rather than literal translation. The phrase אֵ֣לֶּה הׄ שְּׁמוֹת (elleh shemot, 'these are the names') employs the demonstrative pronoun for emphatic introduction, a formulaic structure in genealogical and administrative texts (compare Genesis 5:1; 10:1). The preposition בֹּא (bo, 'coming/entering') in בְּבֹאָם (bevo'am, 'when they came') is a Qal infinitive construct with the 3mp pronominal suffix, indicating contemporaneous action. The Vulgate renders 'qui ingressi sunt' with ingressus, emphasizing the completed action of entry.
crossReferences: Genesis 29:31-30:24; Genesis 35:18-26; Genesis 46:8-27; Genesis 47:11; Deuteronomy 10:22; Acts 7:14; Hebrews 7:14; Revelation 7:4-8; Matthew 1:1-17; Luke 3:23-38.
historicalTrivia: Archaeological excavations at Tell el-Dab'a (identified as Avaris, the Hyksos capital) have revealed extensive Semitic settlement in the eastern Nile Delta dating to the Middle Bronze Age II (c. 2000–1550 BCE). Strontium isotope analysis of teeth from burials at the site indicates that approximately 20% of the population originated in the Levantine highlands, confirming substantial Semitic immigration. The site's palatial complex contains Minoan-style frescoes and an unusual mortuary monument with a statue featuring red-painted skin and a throw-stick—possibly representing a Semitic ruler. Sediment cores from Lake Moeris and the Fayyum depression indicate a period of increased Nile flooding during this era, which would have attracted pastoralists to the well-watered Delta pastures described in Genesis 47:6.

dominicalIntent: The enumeration of Reuben as firstborn establishes the pattern of divine election over primogeniture that culminates in Christ. Reuben's disqualification through incest (Genesis 35:22; 49:4) and the elevation of Judah and Joseph's lines demonstrate that salvation comes through God's sovereign choice, not natural right—a principle fulfilled when the eternal Son assumes humanity not by fleshly descent alone but by the Spirit's operation, and when the 'firstborn' status transfers to the Church, the 'firstborn assembly' (Colossians 1:18; Hebrews 12:23).
cccReferences: CCC 422 (Christ as fulfillment of the promise to Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob); CCC 257 (the divine 'I AM' as source of all being, prefigured in the patriarchal covenant); CCC 705 (the 'God of Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob' as the God of the living, revealed fully in Christ's resurrection).
historicalContext: The tribal structure reflected in the twelve sons corresponds to Iron I ethnographic patterns visible in the hill country of Canaan, though the narrative projects these affiliations back to an earlier period. The name Reuben (רְאוּבֵן, re'uven, 'see, a son') reflects the West Semitic onomastic tradition of theophoric and birth-oracle names. In Egyptian contexts, Semitic names appear in the Execration Texts (Middle Kingdom, c. 2000–1800 BCE) and later in the Amarna letters, demonstrating sustained Semitic presence in Egypt and its environs. The specific tribal arrangement here—six Leah tribes, two Bilhah, two Zilpah, two Rachel—reflects a literary structuring that may preserve memory of matrilineal house divisions within the larger clan.
translationNuances: Hebrew: רְאוּבֵן (re'uven)—the name is a Qal imperative of רָאָה (ra'ah, 'to see') plus the noun בֵּן (ben, 'son'), literally 'see, a son!' The LXX preserves the transliteration Ῥουβήν (Rhoubēn), while the Vulgate offers 'Ruben.' The construct chain בְּנֵי יַעֲקֹב (benei ya'akov, 'sons of Jacob') uses the plural construct of בֵּן with the proper noun, a standard genealogical formula. The waw-consecutive וַיָּבֹא (vayyavo, 'and he came') in some manuscript traditions of related passages indicates narrative progression, though here the text employs nominal clauses (participial/verbless constructions) for stative listing.
crossReferences: Genesis 29:32; Genesis 35:22; Genesis 49:3-4; 1 Chronicles 5:1-2; Hebrews 7:14; Luke 3:33; Matthew 1:2; Deuteronomy 33:6; Numbers 26:5-11.
historicalTrivia: Paleo-Hebrew ostraca from Khirbet Qeiyafa (c. 1000 BCE) and the Tel Zayit abecedary demonstrate the early alphabetic script in which names like Reuben would have been recorded. The name Reuben appears in the Samaria ostraca (8th century BCE) as rwʾbn, confirming long-term tribal memory. Geological surveys of the Negev and Sinai highlands indicate that the period c. 1800–1500 BCE experienced increased precipitation (the 'Middle Bronze Climatic Optimum'), facilitating the pastoral transhumance patterns described in the patriarchal narratives and supporting larger populations of semi-nomadic herders in the regions between Canaan and Egypt.

dominicalIntent: The pairing of Simeon and Levi, instruments of violent zeal (Genesis 34), with Judah, the tribe of kingship, foreshadows the complex working of divine providence. Levi's eventual elevation to priesthood despite his violence, and Judah's emergence as the royal line, point to the Church's teaching on conversion and the transformation of human sin into instruments of grace—fulfilled supremely when Judah's descendant, the Virgin Mary, bears the Messiah, and when Levi's descendant, John the Baptist, prepares His way.
cccReferences: CCC 489 (Mary of the tribe of Judah as the fulfillment of Israel's hope); CCC 2572 (the Levitical priesthood as prefiguring Christ's eternal priesthood); CCC 1544 (the uniqueness of Christ's priesthood fulfilling and transcending the Levitical order); CCC 580 (Christ as the 'son of David' fulfilling the Judahite promise).
historicalContext: The name Issachar (יִשָּׁשכָר, yissakhar) may derive from the West Semitic *šakhar ('hire, reward'), possibly reflecting corvée labor terminology that becomes ironically significant in the exodus narrative. Zebulun (זְבוּלֻן, zevulun) is related to the root ז-ב-ל (z-b-l, 'to dwell, honor'), attested in Ugaritic texts as a divine epithet (zbl, 'prince'). The pairing of Leah's last two sons with her first two creates a literary inclusio. The tribal system reflected here corresponds to territorial patterns visible in the settlement archaeology of the Galilee and Jezreel regions, where Zebulun and Issachar territories were contiguous and agriculturally productive—Zebulun with access to the Mediterranean and Sea of Galilee, Issachar in the fertile valley.
translationNuances: Hebrew: שִׁמְעוֹן (shim'on, 'hearing')—the name is a Qal active participle of שָׁמַע (shama', 'to hear'), referring to Leah's statement 'the Lord has heard' (Genesis 29:33). לֵוִי (levi, 'attached') is a Niphal participle from לָוָה (lavah, 'to join'), Leah's prayer 'my husband will be joined to me' (Genesis 29:34). יְהוּדָה (yehudah, 'praised') is a Hophal/pual form from י-ד-ה (y-d-h, 'to praise'), with the divine name element possibly implied. The LXX renders Συμεών, Λευί, Ἰούδας, Ἰσσαχάρ, Ζαβουλών, with Ζαβουλών representing a different vocalization tradition. The Vulgate's 'Simeon, Levi, Juda, Issachar, Zabulon' preserves Latinized forms. The asyndeton (lack of conjunction) in the Hebrew list creates a staccato, archival effect.
crossReferences: Genesis 29:33-35; Genesis 34:25-31; Genesis 49:5-12; Numbers 26:12-14; Deuteronomy 33:7; Matthew 1:2; Luke 3:30-33; Hebrews 7:14; Revelation 5:5; John 4:22.
historicalTrivia: The Jezreel Valley, core territory of Issachar and Zebulun, has been subject to intensive geoarchaeological survey. Magnetometer surveys and drill cores reveal that the valley's marshy conditions in the Bronze Age required extensive drainage—work that would have been organized by tribal or state authorities. Pollen cores from the Sea of Galilee (Lake Kinneret) indicate that olive cultivation intensified in the Late Bronze and Iron I periods, corresponding to the agricultural wealth implied in Deborah's blessing of Zebulun and Issachar (Judges 5:14-18). Satellite imagery analysis has identified ancient field systems and terracing in the lower Galilee highlands consistent with sustained settlement by these tribal groups from the second millennium BCE onward.

dominicalIntent: The enumeration of Dan and Naphtali reveals Christ's complete assumption of humanity, including tribes marginalized by later Israelite history. Christ gathers the scattered, fulfilling the patriarchal promise that all Israel's branches find unity in Him, the True Vine. The seemingly genealogical list becomes a typological foreshadowing of the Church's catholicity, where no tribe is excluded from redemption.
cccReferences: CCC 422: 'But when the time had fully come, God sent forth his Son, born of woman, born under the law, to redeem those who were under the law, so that we might receive adoption as sons.' The listing of all twelve tribes' progenitors, including Dan and Naphtali, affirms that Christ's redemption encompasses the entirety of Israel's heritage, not merely the politically dominant tribes; CCC 877: The apostolic college with Peter at its head perpetuates this gathering of the complete Israel into the New Covenant.
historicalContext: The tribe of Dan occupied territory in the northernmost reaches of Canaan, bordering Phoenician influence, while Naphtali's territory encompassed the strategic Sea of Galilee region. Both tribes would later be among the first deported by Assyria in 722 BCE, becoming associated with the 'lost tribes.' Their inclusion here, before Egyptian enslavement, establishes their integral place in Israel's foundational identity. The settlement patterns reflect Late Bronze Age population movements and territorial competition among Canaanite city-states and emerging highland settlements.
translationNuances: Hebrew 'דָּן' (Dan) derives from root d-n-n, 'to judge,' reflecting Rachel's maidservant Bilhah's birth narrative (Gen 30:6). 'נַפְתָּלִי' (Naphtali) stems from n-p-l, 'to wrestle,' with Rachel's declaration 'naphtuli elohim' ('wrestlings of God,' Gen 30:8). The LXX reads Δὰν καὶ Νεφθαλεί, with the latter showing the characteristic Greek -ei diphthong rendering of final -i. The Vulgate has 'Dan et Nephthali,' with Jerome maintaining the Hebrew spelling tradition against earlier Latin variants.
crossReferences: Genesis 30:6-8; Genesis 35:25; Genesis 46:23-24; Numbers 1:12,15; Deuteronomy 27:13; Judges 18:1-31; 2 Kings 15:29; Matthew 4:13-15; Revelation 7:6-7
historicalTrivia: Satellite imagery and sediment core analysis from the Sea of Galilee (Lake Kinneret) reveals dramatic Late Bronze Age-Iron I transition settlement abandonment consistent with the period of Egyptian imperial withdrawal from Canaan (ca. 1150 BCE). Pollen cores from the Hula Valley, within Naphtali's traditional territory, indicate significant deforestation and agricultural intensification during this transitional period, suggesting population pressures that may have driven territorial expansion. The Dan stele (ca. 850 BCE), discovered at Tel Dan in 1993, provides the first extrabiblical reference to the 'House of David,' confirming the historical memory of this tribe despite its marginal geographical position.

dominicalIntent: The number seventy encapsulates the totality of nations in Genesis 10, prefiguring Christ's gathering of all nations into the New Israel. Joseph's presence 'already in Egypt' anticipates the prevenient grace that precedes the Incarnation; as Joseph prepared salvation before his brothers' arrival, so Christ precedes us in our Egyptian captivity to sin. The soul count represents complete humanity, body and soul, destined for resurrection.
cccReferences: CCC 60: 'The people descended from Abraham would be the trustee of the promise made to the patriarchs, the chosen people, called to prepare for that day when God would gather all his children into the unity of the Church.' The seventy souls embody this preparatory gathering; CCC 2563: The soul (nephesh) as the seat of life and consciousness, destined for beatific vision, prefigured in this census of Israel's complete vitality.
historicalContext: The number seventy corresponds to the Table of Nations in Genesis 10 and reflects ancient Near Eastern numerical symbolism of completeness. In Egyptian administrative texts, the 'House of Life' (pr-ʿnḫ) associated with temple scriptoria contained idealized lists of knowledge. The Septuagint tradition expands to seventy-two, matching the number of nations and later the apostles sent in Luke 10:1. Demographic estimates for Semitic populations in the eastern Delta during the Hyksos period and later suggest substantial settlement patterns consistent with the narrative's memory of significant Israelite presence.
translationNuances: Hebrew 'נֶפֶשׁ' (nephesh), traditionally 'soul,' more precisely denotes 'living being' or 'vitality,' from root n-p-š, 'to breathe.' The construct phrase 'נֶפֶשׁ יֹצְאֵי יֶרֶךְ' ('souls going out of the thigh/loins') employs euphemistic Hebrew for progeny. LXX: 'ψυχαὶ ἑβδομήκοντα πέντε' (seventy-five souls), harmonizing with Genesis 46:27's expanded count including Joseph's sons born in Egypt. Vulgate: 'septuaginta quinque,' following LXX against MT's seventy.
crossReferences: Genesis 10:1-32; Genesis 46:26-27; Deuteronomy 10:22; Exodus 24:1,9; Numbers 11:16-17; Luke 10:1-17; Acts 7:14; Revelation 7:4-8
historicalTrivia: Papyrus Brooklyn 35.1446, an Egyptian document from ca. 1700 BCE (Middle Kingdom/Second Intermediate Period transition), lists 95 household names of Semitic servants and slaves in Egypt, including characteristically Northwest Semitic names ('Shiphrah,' matching the midwife in Exodus 1:15). This administrative text confirms substantial Semitic populations in Egypt during periods corresponding to the biblical narrative's chronological framework. Stable isotope analysis of remains from Tell el-Dab'a (Avaris), the Hyksos capital in the eastern Delta, reveals dietary patterns consistent with Levantine pastoralists rather than native Egyptians, supporting archaeological evidence for significant Semitic settlement.

dominicalIntent: The death of Joseph marks the end of the patriarchal era and the beginning of Israel's Egyptian sojourn, typologically prefiguring the interval between the Old and New Covenants. Joseph's death before Israel's oppression mirrors the experience of generations awaiting Messiah; yet his embalmed body (Gen 50:26) preserves the promise of resurrection, fulfilled when Moses carries his bones to the Promised Land (Ex 13:19). Christ's own death and burial precede the Exodus of His resurrection.
cccReferences: CCC 641: 'The empty tomb and the linen cloths lying there signify in themselves that by God's power Christ's body had escaped the bonds of death and corruption.' Joseph's preserved body, carried through the wilderness, becomes a material sign of hope in bodily resurrection; CCC 2574: 'Moses the mediator begs the mercy of God, who will have pity on his people and forgive them.' The period between Joseph and Moses represents the silence before the new mediation.
historicalContext: Joseph's death and embalming reflect authentic Egyptian mummification practices, particularly the 70-day mourning period (Gen 50:3) matching known Egyptian customs. The transition from the Hyksos period to the New Kingdom (18th Dynasty) involved significant political realignment, with pharaonic ideology increasingly emphasizing Egyptian ethnic purity and divine kingship. The 'new king who did not know Joseph' (Ex 1:8) likely reflects this ideological shift rather than literal ignorance, as Egyptian kingship propaganda regularly asserted dominance over foreign elements.
translationNuances: Hebrew 'וַיָּמָת' (vayyamot), 'and he died,' employs the standard qal perfect of m-w-t, with paragogic -o- in the narrative (wayyiqtol) form. 'יוֹסֵף' (Yosef) with full spelling (defectiva in some manuscripts). 'וְכָל־אֶחָיו' (vekhol-ʾehav), 'and all his brothers,' with collective singular. LXX: 'Ἰωσὴφ δὲ ἐγένετο ἐν Αἰγύπτῳ, καὶ ἀπέθανεν αὐτὸς καὶ οἱ ἀδελφοὶ αὐτοῦ,' with temporal clause addition. Vulgate: 'Joseph mortuus est et omnes fratres illius,' more concise, with illius for the anaphoric pronoun.
crossReferences: Genesis 50:24-26; Exodus 13:19; Joshua 24:32; Hebrews 11:22; Acts 7:16; Genesis 47:29-30; Deuteronomy 10:6
historicalTrivia: Computed tomography and chemical analysis of mummies from the Valley of the Kings and related New Kingdom sites reveals sophisticated embalming chemistry, including imported resins from the Levant (Pistacia, coniferous pitch) and sub-Saharan Africa. The 70-day embalming period mentioned in Genesis 50:3 corresponds precisely to documented Egyptian practice. DNA analysis of mummies from the New Kingdom period (including KV55 and related remains, ca. 1350-1330 BCE) reveals genetic continuity with earlier populations, while craniofacial reconstruction of Amenhotep III and related individuals shows distinctive prognathism. The transition to the 18th Dynasty involved reconsolidation of Theban power after Hyksos expulsion, with monumental construction at sites including Deir el-Bahari and Karnak reflecting renewed imperial ideology.

dominicalIntent: The fecundity of Israel in Egypt prefigures the Church's supernatural fruitfulness; as Israel multiplied despite oppression, so the Church grows through persecution, fulfilling Christ's promise that the gates of hell shall not prevail against her. This typological abundance echoes the divine command to 'be fruitful and multiply' (Gen 1:28), now fulfilled superabundantly in the New Israel where spiritual progeny are born through baptism.
cccReferences: CCC 60-61 (the patriarchs' faith and God's promise of descendants); CCC 762 (the People of God as the seed of Abraham); CCC 1210 (baptism as spiritual generation); CCC 1656 (the Church as mother and family). The multiplication of Israel demonstrates that salvation history proceeds through divine promise rather than human capability, a pattern fulfilled when Christ makes disciples of all nations.
historicalContext: The Hyksos period (c. 1650-1550 BCE) provides plausible context for Semitic prosperity in Egypt's eastern Delta. The Avaris archaeological site (Tell el-Dab'a) reveals a large Semitic settlement with distinct Levantine architecture, including 'Minoan-style' frescoes and temple structures. Manetho's account (preserved in Josephus, Against Apion I.75-91) describes 'shepherd kings' ruling from Avaris. Population estimates for Goshen suggest carrying capacity supported 20,000-30,000 in the Ramesside period, with sedentary agriculture along the Pelusiac branch of the Nile.
translationNuances: Hebrew וּבְנֵי יִשְׂרָאֵל פָּרוּ וַיִּשְׁרְצוּ וַיִּרְבּוּ וַיַּעַצְמוּ (ûbənê yiśrāʾēl pārû wayyišrəṣû wayyirbû wayyaʿaṣmû): pārû from פָּרָה (pārâ, 'to bear fruit, be fruitful'); yišrəṣû from שָׁרַץ (šāraṣ, 'to swarm, teem,' used in Genesis 1 for aquatic creatures and insects, suggesting almost chaotic abundance); wayyirbû from רָבָה (rābâ, 'to become many, great'); wayyaʿaṣmû from עָצַם (ʿāṣam, 'to be strong, mighty, numerous'). LXX: ἐγένοντο δὲ οἱ υἱοὶ Ισραηλ ἡδρύνθη ('the sons of Israel were strengthened/established'). Vulgate: filii Israël creverunt et quasi germinantes multiplicati sunt ('the sons of Israel grew and like sprouts were multiplied').
historicalTrivia: Sediment core analysis from the Nile Delta (Stanley-Warne, 1998; Krom et al., 2002) reveals dramatic hydrological shifts during the late Bronze Age. The Pelusiac branch, which flowed past Avaris/Pi-Ramesses, experienced severe avulsion and sedimentation after c. 1200 BCE, effectively destroying the harbor infrastructure. This geological catastrophe—documented in strontium isotope ratios and foraminifera assemblages—may underlie the 'Red Sea' tradition's topographical memory. Satellite imagery (Landsat, Corona) identifies the ancient Pelusiac course as a 30-meter depression traceable for 80km east of Tell el-Dab'a.

dominicalIntent: The rise of a new king who 'knew not Joseph' inaugurates the paradigm of worldly powers forgetting their debt to divine providence—a pattern fulfilled when Herod and Pilate, ignorant of Christ's kingship, attempt to destroy him. This forgetfulness is the spiritual blindness of those who 'do not know' (οὐκ οἶδα) in Johannine terms, contrasting with the true knowledge of Christ. The Church's experience under Nero, Diocletian, and successive regimes recapitulates this: each generation must relearn that earthly power is contingent upon divine permission.
cccReferences: CCC 64 (the Church's pilgrimage through persecutions); CCC 731 (the Holy Spirit as witness in times of trial); CCC 2473 (martyrdom as supreme witness); CCC 2596 (God's covenant faithfulness despite human forgetfulness). The 'new king' represents every regime that attempts to sever its dependence on the natural and divine law, a recurring temptation of the City of Man.
historicalContext: The 'new king' (מֶלֶךְ חָדָשׁ, melekh ḥādāš) presents chronological crux. If the Exodus is dated to Ramesses II (1279-1213 BCE) or Merneptah (1213-1203 BCE), the 'new king' could represent a dynastic shift from the 18th to 19th Dynasty (Ahmose I expelling the Hyksos, c. 1550 BCE, is too early). Alternatively, the phrase may indicate a usurper or new dynasty within the 19th Dynasty—Seti I and Ramesses II emphasized their distinctiveness from Akhenaten's Amarna period. The 'forgetting of Joseph' reflects actual Egyptian practice of damnatio memoriae against disfavored predecessors, attested in Thutmose III's erasure of Hatshepsut and Akhenaten's successors' erasure of the Aten heresy.
translationNuances: Hebrew וַיָּקָם מֶלֶךְ־חָדָשׁ עַל־מִצְרָיִם אֲשֶׁר לֹא־יָדַע אֶת־יוֹסֵף (wayyāqām melekh-ḥādāš ʿal-miṣrāyim ʾăšer lōʾ-yādaʿ ʾet-yôsēp): wayyāqām ('arose, stood up') suggests sudden, perhaps violent, accession; ḥādāš ('new') can mean 'fresh, renewed, different in kind'; lōʾ-yādaʿ ('did not know') implies not mere ignorance but willful disregard, breaking covenantal memory. LXX: ἀνέστη δὲ βασιλεὺς ἕτερος ἐπ᾽ Αἴγυπτον ὃς οὐκ ᾔδει τὸν Ιωσηφ ('another/ different king arose'). Vulgate: surrexit autem rex novus super Ægyptum qui ignorabat Iosephum ('a new king arose over Egypt who was ignorant of Joseph').
crossReferences: Genesis 41:39-45; Exodus 2:23; Psalm 83:4-8; Acts 7:18; Hebrews 11:23; Matthew 2:3-18; John 16:3; 1 John 3:1
historicalTrivia: Papyrus Brooklyn 35.1446 (c. 13th century BCE) lists 95 household servants including 43 'Asiatics' (ʿmw) with Northwest Semitic names (Shiphrah, Menahem, Bin-ʿAnat), confirming Semitic presence in Egyptian servile contexts. The 'House of the Harim' (pr-ḫnrt) documents show these workers in textile and agricultural labor. Stable isotope analysis (δ¹⁵N, δ¹³C) of remains from Tell el-Dab'a cemeteries indicates dietary stress among lower-status populations, with C4 plant consumption (millet, sorghum) distinguishing servile from elite diets.

dominicalIntent: The Egyptian fear of Israel's numerical strength and potential alliance with enemies reveals the paranoid logic of the world against the Church: the City of Man perceives the City of God as existential threat precisely because it represents an alternative order of loyalty. Christ's kingdom 'not of this world' (John 18:36) provokes analogous anxiety in all totalitarian systems. The 'crafty' counsel (נִתְחַכְּמָה) against Israel is the proto-type of Herod's massacre and the Sanhedrin's plotting, ultimately frustrated by divine providence that transforms intended evil into salvation's instrument.
cccReferences: CCC 64 (the Church's experience of persecution as sign of fidelity); CCC 2238 (civil authorities' limits regarding divine law); CCC 2473 (martyrdom as participation in Christ's sacrifice); CCC 2608 (Christ's suffering as fulfillment of Israel's suffering). The 'dealing wisely/craftily' (נִתְחַכְּמָה) mirrors the 'wisdom of this world' (1 Cor 1:20) that is foolishness before God.
historicalContext: The 'war scenario' (וְנִלְחַם, wenilḥam) reflects realistic geopolitical anxiety. The Sea Peoples' invasions (c. 1208 BCE under Merneptah, c. 1177 BCE under Ramesses III) demonstrated Egypt's vulnerability to coalition forces. The Hittite-Egyptian treaty (c. 1258 BCE) and subsequent correspondence (Amarna letters, EA) show constant concern about vassal loyalty. The 'mixed multitude' (עֵרֶב רַב, ʿerev rav) of Exodus 12:38 suggests Israel's potential as military auxiliaries or mercenaries—a realistic fear given the Shardana and other 'foreign' units in Egyptian service who later proved unreliable.
translationNuances: Hebrew וַיֹּאמֶר אֶל־עַמּוֹ הִנֵּה עַם בְּנֵי יִשְׂרָאֵל רַב וְעָצוּם מִמֶּנּוּ (wayyōʾmer ʾel-ʿammô hinnê ʿam bənê yiśrāʾēl rav wəʿāṣûm mimmennû): hinnê ('behold, look') introduces dramatic, almost theatrical revelation; rav ('many, great') and ʿāṣûm ('mighty, numerous') form herdiadys emphasizing overwhelming numerical-military power; mimmennû ('from us/more than us') suggests comparative or separative sense—'more numerous than we' or 'apart from us [a threat].' LXX: ἰδοὺ τὸ γένος τῶν υἱῶν Ισραηλ μέγα πλῆθος ('behold the race of the sons of Israel [is] a great multitude'). Vulgate: ecce populus filiorum Israël multus et fortior nobis ('behold the people of the sons of Israel [is] many and stronger than we').
crossReferences: Genesis 15:13; Exodus 1:10; 5:5; 12:38; Numbers 22:3-4; Deuteronomy 7:17; 20:1; 26:5; Psalm 105:24-25; Acts 7:17-19; Revelation 12:1-6,13-17
historicalTrivia: Merneptah Stele (Cairo Museum JE 31408, c. 1208 BCE) provides the first extra-biblical reference to 'Israel' (ysrỉr), describing them as a people (sign-determinative) destroyed in Canaan: 'Israel is laid waste, his seed is not.' This contemporaneous Egyptian perception of Israel as military threat—geographically located in Canaan rather than Egypt—complicates straightforward historical correlation with Exodus narratives, yet confirms the broader pattern of Egyptian-Israelite antagonism. The stele's granite composition (from Aswan quarries, 500km south) and polychrome painted hieroglyphs demonstrate the technological infrastructure of Pharaonic propaganda.

dominicalIntent: 'Come, let us deal shrewdly with them, lest they multiply, and if war breaks out, they join our enemies and fight against us and escape from the land' (*Havah nithchakmah lo pen-yirbeh...*). THE TYRANT'S CRAFTY SCHEME! Pharaoh commands: **'Come, let us deal shrewdly/craftily (*nithchakmah*) with them!'** Fearing they will ally with foreign invaders (like the Hyksos) and escape the land.
cccReferences: CCC 2571 (Crafty persecution against God's people); Ps 105:25; Acts 7:19.
historicalContext: State policy of enslavement and population control.
translationNuances: Hebrew *Havah nithchakmah lo pen-yirbeh ve-hayah ki-thiqre'nah milchamah ve-nosaph gam-hu al-sone'eynu ve-nilcham-banu ve-alah min-ha-aretz*: *nithchakmah* (let us act wisely/craftily/shrewdly, root *chakham*).
historicalTrivia: Acts 7:19 summarizes: 'He dealt craftily (*katasophisamenos*) with our race and forced our fathers to expose their infants'.

dominicalIntent: Therefore they set taskmasters over them to afflict them with heavy burdens. They built for Pharaoh store cities, Pithom and Raamses (*Vayyassimu alav ssarey missim le-ma'an annotho be-ssivlotham vayyiven arey misskenoth le-Phar'oh eth-Pithom ve-eth-Ra'amses*). SLAVE LABOR AND THE PITOM AND RAAMSES STORE CITIES! Pharaoh appoints **taskmasters (*ssarey missim*)** to crush Israel under forced labor (*ssivloth*). Israel builds Pharaoh's fortified **store cities (*arey misskenoth*)**: **PITHOM** (*Pi-Tum* = 'House of Atum') and **RAAMSES** (*Pi-Ramesse* = 'House of Rameses').
cccReferences: CCC 2060 (Enslavement in Egypt as the bondage from which God delivers His people); CCC 2571; Exod 20:2.
historicalContext: State forced-labor system (*corvée / missim*). Construction of Pithom (Tell el-Maskhuta) and Raamses (Qantir / Avaris) in the Delta.
translationNuances: Hebrew *Vayyassimu alav ssarey missim le-ma'an annotho be-ssivlotham vayyiven arey misskenoth le-Phar'oh eth-Pithom ve-eth-Ra'amses*: *ssarey missim* ('chiefs of forced labor/tribute'). *arey misskenoth* ('storage cities').
historicalTrivia: Pithom (Egyptian *Pr-Itm*) and Raamses (Egyptian *Pr-R'-mss*) are major historical Egyptian cities confirmed by 19th-Dynasty inscriptions.

dominicalIntent: But the more they were oppressed, the more they multiplied and the more they spread abroad. And the Egyptians were in dread of the people of Israel (*Ve-kha-asher ye'annu otho ken yirbeh ve-khen yiphrotz...*). THE DIVINE PARADOX: THE MORE OPPRESSED, THE MORE THEY MULTIPLIED! **SUPREME SPIRITUAL LAW**: **'BUT THE MORE THEY WERE OPPRESSED, THE MORE THEY MULTIPLIED AND SPREAD ABROAD!'** (*ken yirbeh ve-khen yiphrotz*). Persecution cannot crush God's Church; trial produces explosive spiritual growth! The Egyptians dread Israel (*vayyaqutzu*).
cccReferences: CCC 852 (Persecution causing the Church to grow: 'The blood of martyrs is the seed of Christians'); CCC 2571; Ps 105:24; Acts 8:1-4.
historicalContext: Failure of forced labor to halt Hebrew population growth.
translationNuances: Hebrew *Ve-kha-asher ye'annu otho ken yirbeh ve-khen yiphrotz vayyaqutzu mi-ppney bney Yisra'el*: *yiphrotz* (burst forth / spread like a flood, root *paratz*). *vayyaqutzu* (they felt disgust/dread/loathing).
crossReferences: Acts 8:1-4; Tertullian's Apology ('The blood of martyrs is seed'); Psalm 105:24; Isaiah 54:3.
historicalTrivia: Tertullian's famous 2nd-century maxim (*Sanguis martyrum semen christianorum*) is the exact New Testament realization of Exodus 1:12!

dominicalIntent: So the Egyptians ruthlessly made the people of Israel serve... The Egyptians escalate to brutal, ruthless labor (*be-pharekh*).
historicalContext: Intensification of slave labor conditions.
translationNuances: Hebrew *Vayya'avidu Mitzrayim eth-bney Yisra'el be-pharekh*: *be-pharekh* (with crushing rigor / severity / ruthlessness).
historicalTrivia: The term *be-pharekh* ('crushing rigor') appears in Leviticus 25:43 forbidding Israelites from ruling over brothers ruthlessly.

dominicalIntent: and made their lives bitter with hard service, in mortar and brick, and in all kinds of work in the field. In all their work they ruthlessly made them serve as slaves (*Vayyamarru eth-chayeyhem be-avodah qashah be-chomer u-vi-lvenim...*). BITTER SLAVERY IN MORTAR AND BRICK! The Egyptians make their lives **bitter (*Vayyamarru*)** with hard labor in **mud-brick making (*chomer u-vlvenim*)** and field labor. **THE PASSOVER MAROR (BITTER HERBS) COMMEMORATES THIS EXACT BITTERNESS!**
cccReferences: CCC 1334 (The Passover meal commemorating the bitterness of Egyptian bondage); CCC 2571; Exod 12:8; Deut 26:6.
historicalContext: Mud-brick manufacturing (*lvenim*) using Nile mud mixed with straw desiccation, as depicted in the Tomb of Rekhmire (c. 1450 BC).
translationNuances: Hebrew *Vayyamarru eth-chayeyhem be-avodah qashah be-chomer u-vi-lvenim u-vkhol-avodah ba-sadeh eth kol-avodatham asher-avdu vahem be-pharekh*: *Vayyamarru* (and they made bitter, root *marar* -> *Maror*!). *chomer* (mortar/clay). *lvenim* (bricks).
historicalTrivia: The Tomb of Rekhmire in Thebes shows Semitic slaves making mud-bricks with the inscription: 'The taskmaster says: The rod is in my hand, be not idle'!

dominicalIntent: Then the king of Egypt said to the Hebrew midwives, one of whom was named Shiphrah and the other Puah... INTRODUCTION OF SHIPHRAH AND PUAH! Pharaoh secretly summons the two chief **Hebrew Midwives**: **SHIPHRAH** (*Shiphrah* = 'Beauty / Brightness') and **PUAH** (*Pu'ah* = 'Splendor / One who Cries Out').
cccReferences: CCC 2571 (The heroic witness of the midwives resisting unjust state tyranny); CCC 2242.
historicalContext: Pharaoh attempting covert state infanticide by ordering midwives to kill newborn Hebrew boys.
translationNuances: Hebrew *Vayyo'mer melekh Mitzrayim la-meyalledoth ha-Ivriyyoth asher shem ha-achath Shiphrah ve-shem ha-shenith Pu'ah*: *ha-meyalledoth* (the midwives). *Shiphrah* (beauty/fairness). *Pu'ah* (splendor/radiance).
historicalTrivia: Scripture preserves the names of these two humble midwives (**Shiphrah and Puah**), while omitting the name of the mighty Pharaoh, proving that God honors the humble over tyrants!

dominicalIntent: 'When you serve as midwife to the Hebrew women and see them on the birthstool, if it is a son, you shall kill him; but if it is a daughter, she shall live' (*im-ben hu ve-hamitthen otho...*). COVERT INFANTICIDE DECREE! Pharaoh commands covert state murder: **'IF IT IS A SON, YOU SHALL KILL HIM!'** (*im-ben hu ve-hamitthen otho*). Satanic assault on the seed of the woman (Gen 3:15) to exterminate the Messianic line!
cccReferences: CCC 2270 (Abhorrence of infanticide and abortion); CCC 2242 (Refusal of obedience to immoral state mandates); CCC 2571; Matt 2:16 (Herod's slaughter of the Innocents).
historicalContext: State-ordered infanticide executed at the birthstool (*ovnayim* = stone birthing stool).
translationNuances: Hebrew *Vayyo'mer be-yalledkhen eth-ha-Ivriyyoth u-re'ithan al-ha-ovnayim im-ben hu ve-hamitthen otho ve-im-bath hi va-chayah*: *ovnayim* (two birthing stones / birthstool). *ve-hamitthen* ('you shall kill him').
crossReferences: Matthew 2:16 (Herod's massacre of the infants in Bethlehem); Genesis 3:15; Revelation 12:4.
historicalTrivia: Herod's slaughter of the male infants of Bethlehem in Matthew 2:16 is the exact New Testament demonic repetition of Pharaoh's decree!

dominicalIntent: But the midwives feared God and did not do as the king of Egypt commanded them, but let the male children live (*Vatthiyrena ha-meyalledoth eth-ha-Elohim ve-lo assu ka-asher dibber alehen... vatthachayeyna eth-ha-yoladhim*). CIVIL DISOBEDIENCE AND THE FEAR OF GOD! **THE SUPREME MODEL OF HOLY RESISTANCE TO IMMORAL LAWS!** Scripture records: **'BUT THE MIDWIVES FEARED GOD (*Vatthiyrena eth-ha-Elohim*), AND DID NOT DO AS THE KING COMMANDED THEM, BUT LET THE MALE CHILDREN LIVE!'** **CCC 2242 CITES THIS MOMENT: WHEN STATE LAWS VIOLATE GOD'S MORAL LAW, CITIZENS MUST OBEY GOD RATHER THAN MEN (ACTS 5:29)!**
cccReferences: CCC 2242 (REFUSAL OF OBEDIENCE TO IMMORAL LAWS: 'We must obey God rather than men', cited from Exod 1:17 and Acts 5:29); CCC 2270; CCC 2095 (Fear of God); Acts 5:29; Dan 3:16-18.
historicalContext: Heroic non-violent civil disobedience by Shiphrah and Puah defying Pharaoh's murder decree.
translationNuances: Hebrew *Vatthiyrena ha-meyalledoth eth-ha-Elohim ve-lo assu ka-asher dibber alehen melekh Mitzrayim vatthachayeyna eth-ha-yoladhim*: *Vatthiyrena... eth-ha-Elohim* ('and the midwives feared God'). *vatthachayeyna* ('and they preserved alive / caused to live').
crossReferences: CCC 2242; Acts 5:29 ('We must obey God rather than men'); Acts 4:19; Daniel 3:16-18; Daniel 6:10; 2 Maccabees 7:2.
historicalTrivia: CCC 2242 explicitly cites Exodus 1:17 as the foundational Old Testament authority for conscientious objection against unjust state laws.

dominicalIntent: So the king of Egypt called the midwives and said to them: 'Why have you done this, and let the male children live?' Pharaoh interrogates the midwives for defying his order.
historicalContext: Interrogation before the throne.
translationNuances: Hebrew *Vayyiqra melekh-Mitzrayim la-meyalledoth vayyo'mer lahen maddua assithen ha-davar ha-zeh vatthachayeyna eth-ha-yoladhim*.
historicalTrivia: The midwives stand calm before the absolute monarch.

dominicalIntent: The midwives said to Pharaoh: 'Because the Hebrew women are not like the Egyptian women, for they are vigorous and give birth before the midwife comes to them' (*ki-chayoth heneth...*). THE MIDWIVES' CLEVER DEFENSE! The midwives explain that Hebrew women are **vigorous / lively (*chayoth*)** and give birth so rapidly that the baby is born before they arrive!
cccReferences: CCC 2488 (Prudent concealment of truth to save innocent life); CCC 2571.
historicalContext: Using Egyptian racial stereotypes regarding Asiatic vigor to protect innocent infants.
translationNuances: Hebrew *Vatto'marna ha-meyalledoth el-Par'oh ki lo kha-nashim ha-Mitzriyyoth ha-Ivriyyoth ki-chayoth heneth be-therem thavo alehen ha-meyalleldeth ve-yaladu*: *chayoth* (lively/vigorous/full of vitality).
historicalTrivia: St. Augustine wrote that their lie was born of love to save innocent life, and God rewarded their mercy.

dominicalIntent: So God dealt well with the midwives. And the people multiplied and grew very strong (*Vayyeytev Elohim la-meyalledoth vayyireb ha-am vayya'atzmu me'od*). GOD REWARDS THE MIDWIVES! Scripture explicitly states: **'SO GOD DEALT WELL WITH THE MIDWIVES!'** (*Vayyeytev Elohim la-meyalledoth*). Under divine favor, Israel continues to multiply and grow exceedingly strong.
cccReferences: CCC 2571 (God blessing those who defend innocent life); Prov 11:18; Heb 6:10.
historicalContext: Divine blessing rewarding moral courage.
translationNuances: Hebrew *Vayyeytev Elohim la-meyalledoth vayyireb ha-am vayya'atzmu me'od*: *Vayyeytev* ('and God dealt well / showed goodness').
historicalTrivia: God's reward *Vayyeytev* proves that defending innocent human life brings divine favor.

dominicalIntent: And because the midwives feared God, he gave them families (*Vayehi ki-yare'u ha-meyalledoth eth-ha-Elohim vayya'as lahem batthim*). GOD BUILDS HOUSES FOR THE MIDWIVES! Because Shiphrah and Puah feared God, **GOD GAVE THEM HOUSES / FAMILIES OF THEIR OWN (*vayya'as lahem batthim*)**! Jewish tradition (Talmud *Sotah* 11b) holds that from Shiphrah (Jochebed) came the Priestly House of Moses and Aaron, and from Puah (Miriam) came the Royal House of King David!
cccReferences: CCC 2571 (Divine blessing granting eternal lineage to the defenders of life); 1 Sam 2:35; 2 Sam 7:11.
historicalContext: God bestowing enduring family lines (*batthim*) on the child-saving midwives.
translationNuances: Hebrew *Vayehi ki-yare'u ha-meyalledoth eth-ha-Elohim vayya'as lahem batthim*: *batthim* ('houses / family lineages').
crossReferences: 2 Samuel 7:11 ('the Lord will make you a house'); 1 Samuel 2:35; Psalm 127:1.
historicalTrivia: The Talmud (*Sotah* 11b) states that *batthim* ('houses') refers to the House of Priesthood (*Levites*) and the House of Kingship (*Davidic line*) bestowed on their descendants!

dominicalIntent: Then Pharaoh commanded all his people: 'Every son that is born to the Hebrews you shall cast into the Nile, but you shall let every daughter live' (*Kol-ha-ben ha-yillod ha-Ye'orah thashlikhuhu ve-khol-ha-bath thachayyun*). OVERT INFANTICIDE DECREE: 'CAST EVERY SON INTO THE NILE!' Frustrated by the midwives, Pharaoh issues a public, empire-wide decree: **'EVERY SON THAT IS BORN TO THE HEBREWS YOU SHALL CAST INTO THE NILE RIVER!'** (*ha-Ye'orah thashlikhuhu*). SATANIC ASSAULT TO DROWN THE MALE INFANTS! Yet God will use the very Nile River of death to float the Ark of Moses, the savior of Israel!
cccReferences: CCC 2270 (Solemn condemnation of state infanticide); CCC 2571; Matt 2:16; Rev 12:4; Exod 2:3.
historicalContext: Empire-wide state genocide decree ordering all Egyptian citizens to throw male Hebrew infants into the Nile River.
translationNuances: Hebrew *Vaytzav Par'oh le-khol-ammo le'mor kol-ha-ben ha-yillod ha-Ye'orah thashlikhuhu ve-khol-ha-bath thachayyun*: *ha-Ye'orah* (into the Nile River). *thashlikhuhu* ('you shall throw/cast him').
historicalTrivia: Pharaoh ordered Hebrew boys to be thrown into the Nile (*ha-Ye'or*); 80 years later, God turned the Nile into blood (Exod 7:20) in divine retribution!

dominicalIntent: Now a man from the house of Levi went and took as his wife a Levite woman (*Vayyelech ish mi-vveyth Levi vayyiqqach eth-bath-Levi*). THE LEVITICAL MARRIAGE OF MOSES' PARENTS! Amram, a man from the priestly house of Levi, marries Jochebed, a daughter of Levi (Exod 6:20). Moses is born from pure priestly Levite lineage.
cccReferences: CCC 2571 (The birth of Moses within the priestly Levite family); Exod 6:20.
historicalContext: Levite lineage: Amram and Jochebed (Exod 6:20; Num 26:59).
translationNuances: Hebrew *Vayyelech ish mi-vveyth Levi vayyiqqach eth-bath-Levi*: *bath-Levi* ('daughter of Levi').
historicalTrivia: Exodus 6:20 explicitly names Moses' parents: Amram and Jochebed.

dominicalIntent: The woman conceived and bore a son, and when she saw that he was a fine child, she hid him three months (*vattar... ki-thov hu vatthatzpnehu sheloshah yerachim*). THE FINE CHILD HIDDEN THREE MONTHS! Jochebed conceives and bears a son. Seeing that he was **a fine / beautiful child (*ki-thov hu*)**, she hides him for **three months** (*sheloshah yerachim*). **CITED IN HEBREWS 11:23 AS AN ACT OF UNBEATABLE FAITH!**
cccReferences: CCC 2571 (The faith of Moses' parents hiding him from Pharaoh's decree); Heb 11:23; Acts 7:20.
historicalContext: Hiding a newborn male infant from Egyptian infanticide inspectors.
translationNuances: Hebrew *Vatthar ha-ishah vatteleth ben vatthere otho ki-thov hu vatthatzpnehu sheloshah yerachim*: *ki-thov hu* ('that he was good/fair/beautiful', LXX *asteios*).
historicalTrivia: Hebrews 11:23 declares: 'By faith Moses, when he was born, was hidden for three months by his parents, because they saw that the child was beautiful (*asteion*), and they were not afraid of the king's edict'.

dominicalIntent: When she could hide him no longer, she took for him a basket made of bulrushes and daubed it with bitumen and pitch. She put the child in it and placed it among the reeds by the river bank (*vatthiqqach-lo thevath gome...*). THE ARK OF REEDS (*THEVAH*)—PREFIGURING NOAH'S ARK AND THE CHURCH! Jochebed constructs a small ark of papyrus reeds (*thevath gome*) daubed with tar and pitch. THIS IS THE EXACT HEBREW WORD FOR NOAH'S ARK (**THEVAH**)! **AS NOAH'S ARK SAVED HUMANITY FROM THE FLOOD, THE ARK OF MOSES SAVES THE PROPHET FROM THE RIVER OF DEATH, PREFIGURING THE HOLY CATHOLIC CHURCH FLOATING UPON THE WATERS OF BAPTISM!**
cccReferences: CCC 845 (The Ark of salvation prefigured by Moses' papyrus ark); CCC 1219 (Baptismal salvation through water); CCC 2571; Gen 6:14.
historicalContext: Papyrus reed vessel (*thevath gome*) sealed with asphalt/bitumen (*chemeyr*) and pitch (*zepheth*), placed among the Nile marsh reeds (*suph*).
translationNuances: Hebrew *Ve-lo-yakhlah od hatzpzino vatthiqqach-lo thevath gome vat-thachmrah va-chemeyr u-va-zepheth vat-tassem bah eth-ha-yeled vat-tassem ba-ssuph al-ssphath ha-Ye'or*: *thevah* (ark/vessel, used ONLY for Noah's Ark and Moses' basket!). *gome* (papyrus reed). *suph* (reeds/rushes).
historicalTrivia: The Hebrew word *thevah* appears in the entire Old Testament ONLY for Noah's Ark (Gen 6-9) and Moses' basket (Exod 2:3), proving the deliberate theological link!

dominicalIntent: And his sister stood at a distance to know what would be done to him (*Vat-thethatzav achotho me-rachoq...*). MIRIAM WATCHING OVER THE ARK! 7-year-old **Miriam** (*achotho*) stands at a distance watching over the floating ark. Sisterly vigilance and intercession.
cccReferences: CCC 2571 (Miriam's watchful intercession); Exod 15:20; Num 26:59.
historicalContext: Miriam watching from behind Nile bank vegetation.
translationNuances: Hebrew *Vat-thethatzav achotho me-rachoq le-de'ah mah-yeya'asseh lo*: *achotho* (his sister, Miriam).
historicalTrivia: Numbers 26:59 explicitly names the three siblings: Aaron, Moses, and Miriam their sister.

dominicalIntent: Now the daughter of Pharaoh came down to bathe at the river, while her young women walked beside the river. She saw the basket among the reeds and sent her servant woman, and she took it (*Vat-thered bath-Par'oh li-rchotz al-ha-Ye'or...*). PHARAOH'S DAUGHTER DISCOVERS THE ARK! Pharaoh's royal daughter comes down to bathe in the sacred Nile, spots the ark (*thevah*) among the reeds, and sends her maiden to retrieve it.
cccReferences: CCC 2571 (God using the tyrant's own daughter to preserve the savior of Israel); Acts 7:21.
historicalContext: Royal princess bathing in private royal Nile enclosures near Avaris/Rameses.
translationNuances: Hebrew *Vat-thered bath-Par'oh li-rchotz al-ha-Ye'or ve-na'arotheha holekhoth al-yad ha-Ye'or vat-there eth-ha-thevah bi-thokh ha-ssuph vat-tishlach eth-amathah vat-tiqqacheha*.
historicalTrivia: Jewish tradition (Josephus, *Antiquities* II.9.5) names Pharaoh's daughter **Thermuthis** (or **Bithiah**, 1 Chron 4:18).

dominicalIntent: When she opened it, she saw the child, and behold, the baby was crying. She took pity on him and said: 'This is one of the Hebrews' children' (*Vat-thiphthach vat-tir'ehu eth-ha-yeled ve-hinneh-na'ar bokheh vat-thachmol alav...*). THE BABY CRYING AND PRINCESS'S COMPASSION! She opens the ark and beholds the crying baby (*na'ar bokheh*). Stirred with **royal compassion (*vat-thachmol*)**, she recognizes: **'This is one of the Hebrews' children!'**
cccReferences: CCC 2571 (Divine compassion moving the heart of the Egyptian princess); Acts 7:21.
historicalContext: Princess recognizing the circumcised Hebrew infant.
translationNuances: Hebrew *Vat-thiphthach vat-tir'ehu eth-ha-yeled ve-hinneh-na'ar bokheh vat-thachmol alav vat-to'mer mi-yeldhey ha-Ivrim zeh*: *vat-thachmol* (and she had pity/compassion, root *chamal*).
historicalTrivia: God used the tears of baby Moses (*na'ar bokheh*) to melt the heart of Pharaoh's daughter!

dominicalIntent: Then his sister said to Pharaoh's daughter: 'Shall I go and call you a nurse from the Hebrew women to nurse the child for you?' Miriam steps out from the reeds and offers to fetch a Hebrew wet-nurse.
historicalContext: Brilliant diplomatic intervention by young Miriam.
translationNuances: Hebrew *Vatto'mer achotho el-bath-Par'oh Ha-elekh ve-qarathi lakh ishah meyniyneth min ha-Ivriyyoth ve-theyniqlakh eth-ha-yaled*.
historicalTrivia: Miriam's quick thinking ensured Moses would be nursed and raised by his own biological mother!

dominicalIntent: And Pharaoh's daughter said to her: 'Go.' So the girl went and called the child's mother (*Vatto'mer-lah bath-Par'oh lechi vattelech ha-almah vat-thiqra eth-em ha-yaled*). JOCHEBED HIRED TO NURSE HER OWN SON! Pharaoh's daughter agrees. Miriam fetches **Jochebed** (*em ha-yaled* = the child's mother). Divine irony!
cccReferences: CCC 2571 (God's providence restoring the infant to his mother's arms).
historicalContext: Biological mother hired as royal wet-nurse.
translationNuances: Hebrew *Vatto'mer-lah bath-Par'oh lechi vattelech ha-almah vat-thiqra eth-em ha-yaled*: *ha-almah* (the maiden/young woman).
historicalTrivia: Jochebed was paid by Pharaoh's treasury to nurse her own son!

dominicalIntent: And Pharaoh's daughter said to her: 'Take this child away and nurse him for me, and I will give you your wages.' So the woman took the child and nursed him. Jochebed receives state wages to nurse Moses in his early years, instilling in him the covenant faith of Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob.
cccReferences: CCC 2571 (Early formation in covenant faith by Jochebed); Heb 11:24-26.
historicalContext: Royal nursing contract lasting 2 to 3 years before weaning.
translationNuances: Hebrew *Vatto'mer lah bath-Par'oh Heylikhi eth-ha-yeled ha-zeh ve-heyniqi-hu li va-ani etten eth-sskharakh vatthiqqach ha-ishah ha-yeled vat-theyniqehu*.
historicalTrivia: During these weaning years, Jochebed secretly taught young Moses his true Hebrew identity and covenant heritage.

dominicalIntent: When the child grew older, she brought him to Pharaoh's daughter, and he became her son. She named him Moses, 'Because,' she said, 'I drew him out of the water' (*Vattiqra shemo Moshe vatyo'mer ki min-ha-mayim meshithihu*). NAMING MOSES: 'DRAWN OUT OF THE WATER'! Upon weaning, he is brought to court and adopted by Pharaoh's daughter. She names him **MOSES** (**Moshe** = 'Drawn Out of the Water'). **MOSES PREFIGURES JESUS CHRIST: DRAWN OUT OF THE WATERS OF DEATH TO BECOME THE REDEEMER OF HIS PEOPLE!**
cccReferences: CCC 2571 (Moses drawn from the water prefiguring Baptism and Christ's salvation); Acts 7:21-22; Heb 11:24.
historicalContext: Egyptian royal adoption. *Moshe* (Egyptian *Msy* / *Mose* = 'Born / Son of', as in Thutmose/Rameses; Hebrew folk etymology *Moshe* = 'Drawn out', from *mashah* = to draw out).
translationNuances: Hebrew *Vayyigdal ha-yeled vat-tevay'ehu le-vath-Par'oh vayyehi-lah le-ven vattiqra shemo Moshe vatyo'mer ki min-ha-mayim meshithihu*: *Moshe* (Drawn out, root *mashah*).
historicalTrivia: Acts 7:22 notes: 'Moses was instructed in all the wisdom of the Egyptians (*epaideuthē Mosēs pasē sophia Aigyptiōn*), and he was mighty in his words and deeds'.

dominicalIntent: One day, when Moses had grown up, he went out to his people and looked on their burdens, and he saw an Egyptian beating a Hebrew, one of his people (*Vayehi ba-yamim ha-hem vayyigdal Moshe vayyetze el-achav vayyar be-ssivlotham...*). MOSES CHOOSES HIS OPPRESSED BRETHREN! 40-year-old Moses goes out from the palace to inspect his Hebrew brothers (*achav*). Seeing an Egyptian striking a Hebrew, **he chooses to side with his oppressed people over the riches of Egypt!**
cccReferences: CCC 2571 (Moses refusing royal Egyptian status to suffer with God's people); Heb 11:24-26; Acts 7:23-24.
historicalContext: Moses at age 40 (Acts 7:23) inspecting the slave brickyards.
translationNuances: Hebrew *Vayehi ba-yamim ha-hem vayyigdal Moshe vayyetze el-achav vayyar be-ssivlotham vayyar ish Mitzri makkeh ish-Ivri me-achav*: *ssivlotham* ('their heavy burdens').
historicalTrivia: Hebrews 11:24-25 praises this moment: 'By faith Moses, when he was grown up, refused to be called the son of Pharaoh's daughter, choosing rather to share ill-treatment with the people of God'.

dominicalIntent: He looked this way and that, and seeing no one, he struck down the Egyptian and hid him in the sand (*Vayyiphen kho va-kho vayyar ki eyn ish vayyakh eth-ha-Mitzri vaythmenehu ba-chol*). SLAYING THE EGYPTIAN TASKMASTER! Moses looks around, sees no one, slays the brutal Egyptian taskmaster, and buries him in the sand. Moses attempts to deliver Israel by human violence, learning that salvation comes only through God's power.
cccReferences: CCC 2571 (Human zeal failing before divine appointment); Acts 7:24-25.
historicalContext: Intervening to avenge an abused Hebrew slave.
translationNuances: Hebrew *Vayyiphen kho va-kho vayyar ki eyn ish vayyakh eth-ha-Mitzri vaythmenehu ba-chol*: *vaythmenehu* (and he hid/buried him).
historicalTrivia: Acts 7:25 notes: 'He supposed that his brothers would understand that God was giving them salvation by his hand, but they did not understand'.

dominicalIntent: When he went out the next day, behold, two Hebrews were struggling together. And he said to the man in the wrong: 'Why do you strike your companion?' Rebuking an aggressive Hebrew who was assaulting his fellow Israelite.
historicalContext: Moses acting as peacemaker among his own people.
translationNuances: Hebrew *Vayyetze ba-yom ha-sheni ve-hinneh sheney-anashim Ivrim nitzim vayyo'mer la-rasha lammah thakkeh re'ekha*: *la-rasha* ('to the wicked/wrong one').
historicalTrivia: Acts 7:26 records: 'He appeared to them as they were quarreling and tried to reconcile them, saying, "Men, you are brothers; why do you wrong each other?"'.

dominicalIntent: He answered: 'Who made you a prince and a judge over us? Do you mean to kill me as you killed the Egyptian?' Then Moses was afraid, and thought: 'Surely the thing is known' (*Mi samkha le-ish sar ve-shophet alenu...*). REJECTION OF THE DELIVERER: 'WHO MADE YOU A PRINCE AND A JUDGE OVER US?' The rebellious Israelite rejects Moses: **'WHO MADE YOU A PRINCE AND A JUDGE OVER US?!'** This exact rejection prefigures **the Jewish leaders rejecting Jesus Christ** ('We have no king but Caesar!', John 19:15; Acts 7:27-28; Acts 7:35)!
cccReferences: CCC 2571 (Rejection of the deliverer prefiguring the rejection of Christ); Acts 7:27-28; Acts 7:35; John 1:11; John 19:15.
historicalContext: Rejection of Moses' unauthorized judicial intervention.
translationNuances: Hebrew *Vayyo'mer mi samkha le-ish sar ve-shophet alenu ha-lehorgheni attah omer ka-asher haraghta eth-ha-Mitzri vayyira Moshe vayyo'mer akhen noda ha-davar*: *sar ve-shophet* ('prince and judge').
crossReferences: Acts 7:27-28; Acts 7:35 ('This Moses, whom they rejected, saying, "Who made you a ruler and a judge?"—this man God sent as both ruler and redeemer'); John 1:11.
historicalTrivia: Acts 7:35 directly quotes this verse to prove that Israel historically rejected its God-given deliverers before accepting them!

dominicalIntent: When Pharaoh heard of it, he sought to kill Moses. But Moses fled from Pharaoh and stayed in the land of Midian. And he sat down by a well (*Vayyishmach Par'oh... vayyivrach Moshe... vayyeshev al-ha-b'er*). FLIGHT TO MIDIAN AND THE WELL! Pharaoh seeks to execute Moses for treason. Moses **flees to the Land of Midian** (Northwestern Arabian Peninsula) and **sits down by a well (*ha-b'er*)**.
cccReferences: CCC 2571 (Moses fleeing to Midian for 40 years of wilderness refining); Acts 7:29; Heb 11:27.
historicalContext: Flight across the Sinai Peninsula into the desert land of Midian (east of the Gulf of Aqaba). Sitting by the well, the traditional patriarchal courting site!
translationNuances: Hebrew *Vayyishma Par'oh eth-ha-davar ha-zeh vayveqesh li-hrogh eth-Moshe vayyivrach Moshe mi-ppney Par'oh vayyeshev be-eretz-Midyan vayyeshev al-ha-b'er*: *ha-b'er* (the well).
historicalTrivia: The 'Well' (*ha-b'er*) is the third major patriarchal well scene in Genesis/Exodus (Abraham's servant for Rebekah in Gen 24, Jacob for Rachel in Gen 29, Moses for Zipporah in Exod 2)!

dominicalIntent: Now the priest of Midian had seven daughters, and they came and drew water and filled the troughs to water their father's flock (*U-le-khohen Midyan sheva banoth...*). Introduction of **Reuel / Jethro**, the monotheistic **Priest of Midian (*Kohen Midyan*)**, whose 7 daughters come to water their sheep.
cccReferences: CCC 2571 (The Priest of Midian and non-Israelite monotheism); Exod 3:1; Exod 18:1.
historicalContext: Reuel (Jethro), a descendant of Abraham through Keturah (Gen 25:2), serving as a monotheistic patriarch-priest in Midian.
translationNuances: Hebrew *U-le-khohen Midyan sheva banoth vat-thavo'nah vat-thidlenah vat-thimmale'nah eth-ha-rrhatim le-hashqoth tzon avihen*: *ha-rrhatim* (the watering troughs).
historicalTrivia: Midianites descended from Abraham and Keturah (Gen 25:2), preserving ancient patriarchal worship of God.

dominicalIntent: The shepherds came and drove them away, but Moses stood up and saved them, and watered their flock (*vayyaqam Moshe vayyoshi'an vayyashq eth-tzonam*). MOSES DELIVERS THE DAUGHTERS AT THE WELL! Hostile shepherds drive the 7 maidens away. Moses steps in, **rescues/saves them (*vayyoshi'an*)**, and waters their flock! Moses acts again as a deliverer (*yasha*).
cccReferences: CCC 2571 (Moses as protector and savior of the weak).
historicalContext: Defending young women against aggressive desert herdsmen.
translationNuances: Hebrew *Vayyavo'u ha-ro'im vaygharrshum vayyaqam Moshe vayyoshi'an vayyashq eth-tzonam*: *vayyoshi'an* (and he saved/delivered them, root *yasha* -> *Yeshua*!).
historicalTrivia: The verb *vayyoshi'an* ('and he saved them') uses the exact root of **Jesus / Yeshua** (*salvation*)!

dominicalIntent: When they came home to their father Reuel, he said: 'How is it that you have come back so soon today?' Their father **Reuel** (*Re'u'el* = 'Friend of God') expresses surprise at their quick return.
historicalContext: Arrival at the Midianite family encampment.
translationNuances: Hebrew *Vatthavo'nah el-Re'u'el avihen vayyo'mer Maddua miharthen bo ha-yom*: *Re'u'el* ('Friend of God').
historicalTrivia: Reuel is also called **Jethro** (*Yithro* = 'His Excellence', Exod 3:1), likely his official title as High Priest of Midian.

dominicalIntent: They said: 'An Egyptian delivered us out of the hand of the shepherds and even drew water for us and watered the flock' (*Ish Mitzri hitzilanu mi-yad ha-ro'im...*). THEY REPORT: 'AN EGYPTIAN DELIVERED US!' The daughters describe Moses as **'An Egyptian man (*Ish Mitzri*)'** because of his Egyptian attire, speech, and appearance.
historicalContext: Moses still wearing his royal Egyptian court garments.
translationNuances: Hebrew *Vatto'marna ish Mitzri hitzilanu mi-yad ha-ro'im ve-gham-dalah dalah lanu vayyashq eth-ha-tzon*: *hitzilanu* (he delivered us, root *natzal*).
historicalTrivia: Moses is called 'an Egyptian' (*Ish Mitzri*) here, but later becomes the ultimate liberator *from* Egypt!

dominicalIntent: He said to his daughters: 'And where is he? Why have you left the man? Call him, that he may eat bread.' Reuel rebukes his daughters for leaving their savior at the well and extends desert hospitality.
historicalContext: Desert hospitality inviting the stranger to break bread.
translationNuances: Hebrew *Vayyo'mer el-bnothav ve-ayyo lammah zeh azavten eth-ha-ish qir'an lo ve-yo'khal lechem*.
historicalTrivia: Luke 24:29 ('Abide with us, for it is toward evening') mirrors Reuel inviting the savior to break bread.

dominicalIntent: And Moses was content to dwell with the man, and he gave Moses his daughter Zipporah (*Vayyo'el Moshe la-sheveth eth-ha-ish vayyitten eth-Tzipporah vintho le-Moshe*). MARRIAGE TO ZIPPORAH! Moses agrees to dwell with Reuel, and receives his daughter **ZIPPORAH** (*Tzipporah* = 'Little Bird / Bird') in marriage.
cccReferences: CCC 2571 (Moses' marriage in Midian during his 40-year wilderness shepherd training).
historicalContext: Moses settling down as a shepherd in Midian.
translationNuances: Hebrew *Vayyo'el Moshe la-sheveth eth-ha-ish vayyitten eth-Tzipporah vintho le-Moshe*: *Tzipporah* (bird/sparrow).
historicalTrivia: Zipporah (*Tzipporah*) later plays a crucial role in saving Moses' life through emergency circumcision in Exod 4:25!

dominicalIntent: She gave birth to a son, and he called his name Gershom, for he said: 'I have been a sojourner in a foreign land' (*Gher hayithi be-eretz nokhriyyah*). BIRTH OF GERSHOM! Zipporah bears Moses a son. Moses names him **GERSHOM** (*Gershom* = 'Sojourner There / Exile'). He testifies: **'I HAVE BEEN A SOJOURNER IN A FOREIGN LAND!'** (*Gher hayithi be-eretz nokhriyyah*).
cccReferences: CCC 2571 (Moses experiencing exile and sojourning in Midian); Heb 11:13.
historicalContext: Birth of Moses' firstborn son in Midian.
translationNuances: Hebrew *Vatteleth ben vayyiqra eth-shemo Gershom ki amar gher hayithi be-eretz nokhriyyah*: *Gershom* (from *ger* = sojourner + *sham* = there).
historicalTrivia: Acts 7:29 notes: 'At this retort Moses fled and became an exile (*paroikos*) in the land of Midian, where he became the father of two sons'.

dominicalIntent: During those many days the king of Egypt died, and the people of Israel groaned because of their slavery and cried out. Their cry for rescue came up to God out of their slavery (*Vayyena'achu bney-Yisra'el min-ha-avodah vayyiz'aqu vat-ta'al shav'atham el-ha-Elohim*). THE GROANING OF ISRAEL REACHES GOD! 40 years pass; Pharaoh dies. Israel groans under crushing slavery and **cries out** (*vayyiz'aqu*). **THEIR CRY FOR HELP ASCENDS DIRECTLY TO GOD (*vat-ta'al shav'atham el-ha-Elohim*)!**
cccReferences: CCC 2572 (The prayer of the oppressed ascending to God and initiating the Exodus redemption); CCC 2571; Exod 3:7-9; Ps 102:19-20.
historicalContext: Death of Pharaoh (Thutmose III c. 1425 BC). Continued brutal state labor under his successor.
translationNuances: Hebrew *Vayehi va-yamim ha-rabbim ha-hem vayyamoth melekh Mitzrayim vayyena'achu bney-Yisra'el min-ha-avodah vayyiz'aqu vat-ta'al shav'atham el-ha-Elohim min-ha-avodah*: *shav'atham* ('their cry for help / petition').
historicalTrivia: James 5:4 echoes this: 'The cries of the harvesters have reached the ears of the Lord of hosts'.

dominicalIntent: And God heard their groaning, and God remembered his covenant with Abraham, with Isaac, and with Jacob (*Vayyishma Elohim eth-na meqatham vayyizkor Elohim eth-beritho eth-Avraham eth-Yitzchaq ve-eth-Ya'aqov*). GOD HEARS AND REMEMBERS HIS COVENANT! FOUR SAVING ACTIONS OF GOD BEGIN! (1) **God HEARD (*Vayyishma*) their groaning**, (2) **God REMEMBERED (*Vayyizkor*) His covenant with Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob!** Divine memory is not passive recall, but active covenant intervention!
cccReferences: CCC 2063 (God remembering His covenant to liberate His people); CCC 2571; CCC 2572; Ps 105:8; Ps 106:44-45; Luke 1:72.
historicalContext: The divine initiative of the Exodus grounded in the Abrahamic Covenant.
translationNuances: Hebrew *Vayyishma Elohim eth-na meqatham vayyizkor Elohim eth-beritho eth-Avraham eth-Yitzchaq ve-eth-Ya'aqov*: *na meqatham* (their groaning/sighing). *vayyizkor* (and He remembered).
crossReferences: Luke 1:72 ('to remember his holy covenant'); Psalm 105:8; Psalm 106:44-45; Exodus 6:5.
historicalTrivia: Luke 1:72 in Zechariah's *Benedictus* quotes Exodus 2:24 word-for-word: 'to show mercy promised to our fathers and to remember his holy covenant'!

dominicalIntent: God saw the people of Israel—and God knew (*Vayyar Elohim eth-bney Yisra'el vayyeda Elohim*). GOD SEES AND GOD KNOWS! The final 2 saving actions of God: (3) **God SAW (*Vayyar*) the people of Israel**, (4) **GOD KNEW! (*Vayyeda Elohim*)**. God's intimate, loving knowledge (*yada*) of His suffering people launches the entire drama of Redemption and the Burning Bush in Exodus 3!
cccReferences: CCC 2572 (God's intimate knowledge of human suffering initiating salvation); CCC 2571; Exod 3:7; Ps 139:1-2; John 10:14.
historicalContext: The climax of Exodus 2 preparing for the Burning Bush calling of Moses in Exodus 3.
translationNuances: Hebrew *Vayyar Elohim eth-bney Yisra'el vayyeda Elohim*: *vayyeda* (and He knew / took intimate personal knowledge of, root *yada*).
crossReferences: Exodus 3:7 ('I know their sufferings'); Psalm 139:1-2; John 10:14 ('I know my own and my own know me'); Nahum 1:7.
historicalTrivia: The 4 verbs of Exodus 2:24-25—**Heard, Remembered, Saw, Knew**—form the foundational four pillars of biblical theology on Divine Redemption!

dominicalIntent: Now Moses was keeping the flock of his father-in-law, Jethro, the priest of Midian, and he led his flock to the west side of the wilderness and came to Horeb, the mountain of God (*U-Moshe hayah ro'eh eth-tzon Yithro chothno khohen Midyan... vayyavo el-har ha-Elohim Chorevah*). MOSES THE SHEPHERD AT MOUNT HOREB! 80-year-old Moses is pasturing the flock of **Jethro (*Yithro*)** in the wilderness. He leads the flock to the back of the desert and arrives at **HOREB, THE MOUNTAIN OF GOD** (*har ha-Elohim Chorevah* = Mount Sinai). **40 YEARS OF WILDERNESS SHEPHERDING PREPARED MOSES TO SHEPHERD ISRAEL OUT OF EGYPT!**
cccReferences: CCC 2575 (Moses called by God while keeping the flock at Horeb); CCC 2574; Exod 19:1-3; Acts 7:30.
historicalContext: 40 years after fleeing Egypt (Acts 7:30). Mount Horeb (Sinai peninsula), sacred mountain of God.
translationNuances: Hebrew *U-Moshe hayah ro'eh eth-tzon Yithro chothno khohen Midyan vayyinhag eth-ha-tzon achar ha-midbar vayyavo el-har ha-Elohim Chorevah*: *Chorevah* (Horeb = 'Desolation / Waste'). *har ha-Elohim* ('mountain of God').
historicalTrivia: Horeb and Sinai refer to the same sacred mountain range where God gave the Law.

dominicalIntent: And the Angel of the Lord appeared to him in a flame of fire out of the midst of a bush. He looked, and behold, the bush was burning, yet it was not consumed (*Vayyera Mal'akh YHVH elav be-labbath-esh mi-thokh ha-sseneh... ve-ha-sseneh eynennu ukkal*). THE BURNING BUSH (*HA-SSENEH*)—PREFIGURING THE VIRGIN MARY AND THE INCARNATION! The **Angel of Yahweh (*Mal'akh YHVH*)** appears in a blazing flame of fire (*labbath-esh*) out of a thornbush (**sseneh**). The bush burns continuously without being consumed! **PATRISTIC & CATECHETICAL TRADITION DECLARES THE BURNING BUSH TO BE THE PREEMINENT TYPE OF THE BLESSED VIRGIN MARY (SANCTA MARIA IN BURNING BUSH): BEARING THE CONSUMING FIRE OF THE DIVINE LOGOS IN HER WOMB WITHOUT LOSS OF HER VIRGINITY!**
cccReferences: CCC 2575 (The manifestation of God in the burning bush revealing His presence); CCC 495 (Mary as the Burning Bush bearing the Divine Fire); Acts 7:30-31; Mark 12:26; Deut 33:16.
historicalContext: Theophanic revelation of God in the *sseneh* (thorny acacia bush).
translationNuances: Hebrew *Vayyera Mal'akh YHVH elav be-labbath-esh mi-thokh ha-sseneh vayyar ve-hinneh ha-sseneh bo'er ba-esh ve-ha-sseneh eynennu ukkal*: *Mal'akh YHVH* ('Angel of the LORD'). *sseneh* (thornbush / acacia). *eynennu ukkal* ('was not consumed').
historicalTrivia: Eastern Orthodox and Catholic liturgies sing: 'As the Bush burned with fire yet was not consumed, so as a Virgin you gave birth and remained a Virgin!'

dominicalIntent: And Moses said: 'I will turn aside to see this great sight, why the bush is not burned' (*Assurah-na ve-er'eh eth-ha-mar'eh ha-ggadol ha-zeh...*). MOSES TURNS ASIDE IN CONTEMPLATION! Moses pauses his work to contemplate the **great vision (*ha-mar'eh ha-ggadol*)**. Contemplation precedes divine vocation.
cccReferences: CCC 2575 (Contemplative awe opening the heart to divine revelation).
historicalContext: Moses stepping off the path to investigate the supernatural phenomenon.
translationNuances: Hebrew *Vayyo'mer Moshe assurah-na ve-er'eh eth-ha-mar'eh ha-ggadol ha-zeh maddua lo-yiv'ar ha-sseneh*: *ha-mar'eh ha-ggadol* ('this great sight/vision').
historicalTrivia: Acts 7:31 notes: 'When Moses saw it, he marveled at the sight, and as he drew near to look, there came the voice of the Lord'.

dominicalIntent: When the Lord saw that he turned aside to see, God called to him out of the bush: 'Moses, Moses!' And he said: 'Here I am' (*Vayyiqra elav Elohim mi-thokh ha-sseneh vayyo'mer Moshe Moshe vayyo'mer Hinneni*). THE DOUBLE CALL: 'MOSES, MOSES!' AND 'HERE I AM!' Seeing Moses turn aside, God calls out from the burning bush: **'MOSES, MOSES!'** Moses instantly responds with the supreme word of patriarchic obedience: **'HERE I AM!' (*Hinneni*)**.
cccReferences: CCC 2575 (God calling Moses by name and receiving the answer of faith: *Hinneni*); CCC 2577; Gen 22:1; 1 Sam 3:4.
historicalContext: Personal divine vocation from the midst of the burning bush.
translationNuances: Hebrew *Vayyar YHVH ki ssar lir'oth vayyiqra elav Elohim mi-thokh ha-sseneh vayyo'mer Moshe Moshe vayyo'mer Hinneni*: *Hinneni* ('Here I am!').
historicalTrivia: The double invocation ('Moses, Moses!') signifies absolute urgency and intimate election (cf. 'Abraham, Abraham!' Gen 22:11; 'Saul, Saul!' Acts 9:4).

dominicalIntent: Then he said: 'Do not come near; take your sandals off your feet, for the place on which you are standing is holy ground' (*Shal-ne'aleykha me-al ragleykha ki ha-mmaqom... admath-qodesh hu*). TAKE OFF YOUR SANDALS—HOLY GROUND (*ADMATH-QODESH*)! God commands: **'TAKE OFF YOUR SANDALS FROM YOUR FEET, FOR THE PLACE ON WHICH YOU STAND IS HOLY GROUND!'** (*admath-qodesh hu*). **FIRST BIBLICAL REVELATION OF HOLINESS (*QODESH*) IN SACRED SPACE!** Reverence required before the Divine Presence.
cccReferences: CCC 2575 (Sacred reverence before God's holy presence); CCC 2086; Acts 7:33; Josh 5:15.
historicalContext: Removing shoes as a universal ancient Near Eastern gesture of purity and reverence before entering a sacred sanctuary.
translationNuances: Hebrew *Vayyo'mer al-thiqrav halom shal-ne'aleykha me-al ragleykha ki ha-mmaqom asher attha omad alav admath-qodesh hu*: *admath-qodesh* ('ground of holiness / holy ground').
crossReferences: Joshua 5:15 (Commander of the Lord's army to Joshua); Acts 7:33; Exodus 19:12; Ecclesiastes 5:1.
historicalTrivia: Removing shoes remains standard reverential practice in Eastern Christian sanctuaries and Jewish/Semitic sacred spaces.

dominicalIntent: And he said: 'I am the God of your father, the God of Abraham, the God of Isaac, and the God of Jacob.' And Moses hid his face, for he was afraid to look at God (*Anochi Elohey avikha Elohey Avraham Elohey Yitzchaq v-Elohey Ya'aqov...*). THE GOD OF ABRAHAM, ISAAC, AND JACOB—CITED BY JESUS TO PROVE THE RESURRECTION OF THE DEAD! God reveals Himself as the personal Covenant God: **'I AM THE GOD OF YOUR FATHER, THE GOD OF ABRAHAM, THE GOD OF ISAAC, AND THE GOD OF JACOB!'** **JESUS QUOTES THIS EXACT VERSE IN MATTHEW 22:32 TO CONFOUND THE SADDUCEES: 'HE IS NOT GOD OF THE DEAD, BUT OF THE LIVING!'**
cccReferences: CCC 205 (THE GOD OF THE LIVING: Jesus quoting Exod 3:6 to reveal eternal life and resurrection); CCC 207; CCC 2575; Matt 22:32; Mark 12:26-27; Luke 20:37-38; Acts 3:13.
historicalContext: Divine self-identification linking Horeb directly to the Abrahamic Covenant.
translationNuances: Hebrew *Vayyo'mer Anochi Elohey avikha Elohey Avraham Elohey Yitzchaq v-Elohey Ya'aqov vayyassther Moshe panav ki yare me-habbit el-ha-Elohim*: *vayyassther... panav* ('and Moses hid his face').
crossReferences: Matthew 22:32; Mark 12:26-27; Luke 20:37-38; Acts 3:13; Acts 7:32; 1 Kings 19:13.
historicalTrivia: In Matthew 22:32, Jesus proves the Resurrection of the Dead from the Pentateuch using Exodus 3:6: because Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob are dead physically, yet God *is* (present tense) their God, they are alive unto Him!

dominicalIntent: Then the Lord said: 'I have surely seen the affliction of my people who are in Egypt and have heard their cry because of their taskmasters. I know their sufferings...' (*Ra'oh ra'ithi eth-oni ammi... yada'ti eth-makh'ovav*). DIVINE COMPASSION: 'I HAVE SEEN, I HAVE HEARD, I KNOW THEIR SUFFERINGS!' Yahweh announces: (1) **'I have surely seen (*Ra'oh ra'ithi*) the affliction of my people'**, (2) **'I have heard their cry'**, (3) **'I KNOW THEIR SUFFERINGS (*yada'ti eth-makh'ovav*)!'** God's heart beats with love for the suffering.
cccReferences: CCC 2575 (God's compassionate initiative to deliver His suffering people); CCC 2063; Exod 2:24-25; Isa 63:9.
historicalContext: Divine response to Hebrew slave cries in Egypt.
translationNuances: Hebrew *Vayyo'mer YHVH ra'oh ra'ithi eth-oni ammi asher be-Mitzrayim ve-eth-tza'aqatham shama'ti mi-ppney noghssav ki yada'ti eth-makh'ovav*: *Ra'oh ra'ithi* (infinitive absolute: 'seeing I have surely seen!'). *makh'ovav* ('their deep pains/sorrows').
historicalTrivia: Acts 7:34 quotes this: 'I have surely seen the affliction of my people who are in Egypt, and have heard their groaning, and I have come down to deliver them'.

dominicalIntent: '...and I have come down to deliver them out of the hand of the Egyptians and to bring them up out of that land to a good and broad land, a land flowing with milk and honey...' (*ve-ered le-hattzilo... el-eretz zavath chalav u-dvash*). THE PROMISED LAND FLOWING WITH MILK AND HONEY! God announces His intervention: **'I HAVE COME DOWN TO DELIVER THEM (*ve-ered le-hattzilo*)'** and bring them to **'A LAND FLOWING WITH MILK AND HONEY (*eretz zavath chalav u-dvash*)'**! THIS IS THE FIRST BIBLICAL APPEARANCE OF THE FAMOUS TITLE 'A LAND FLOWING WITH MILK AND HONEY'!
cccReferences: CCC 2063 (God coming down to liberate His people and give them the Promised Land); CCC 2575; Lev 20:24; Deut 6:3.
historicalContext: The promise of Canaan's rich agricultural fertility.
translationNuances: Hebrew *ve-ered le-hattzilo mi-yad Mitzrayim u-le-ha'alotho min-ha-aretz ha-hi el-eretz tovah u-rhavah el-eretz zavath chalav u-dvash...*: *zavath chalav u-dvash* ('flowing/gushing with milk and honey').
historicalTrivia: Milk (*chalav*) represented rich pastoral livestock abundance, while honey (*dvash*) represented rich fruit/date-syrup agricultural abundance.

dominicalIntent: 'And now, behold, the cry of the people of Israel has come to me, and I have also seen the oppression with which the Egyptians oppress them.' Re-affirming that Israel's cry has ascended to the throne of God.
historicalContext: Divine judicial hearing of the cry of the oppressed.
translationNuances: Hebrew *Ve-attah hinneh tza'aqath bney-Yisra'el ba'ah elai ve-gham-ra'ithi eth-ha-llachatz asher Mitzrayim lochatzim otham*: *llachatz* (crushing oppression/squeeze).
historicalTrivia: The noun *lachatz* means a tight, crushing pressure.

dominicalIntent: 'Come, I will send you to Pharaoh that you may bring my people, the children of Israel, out of Egypt' (*Ve-attah lekhah ve-eshlachakha el-Par'oh ve-hotze eth-ammi bney-Yisra'el mi-Mitzrayim*). THE COMMISSION OF MOSES AS REDEEMER! God commands 80-year-old Moses: **'COME, I WILL SEND YOU TO PHARAOH THAT YOU MAY BRING MY PEOPLE OUT OF EGYPT!'** Moses receives his official prophetic commission.
cccReferences: CCC 2575 (Moses commissioned as the mediator of liberation); CCC 2063; Acts 7:34; Heb 11:27.
historicalContext: Prophetic call and sending (*shelichuth*).
translationNuances: Hebrew *Ve-attah lekhah ve-eshlachakha el-Par'oh ve-hotze eth-ammi bney-Yisra'el mi-Mitzrayim*: *eshlachakha* ('I will send you', root *shalach* -> Apostle/Sent One!).
crossReferences: Acts 7:34; Micah 6:4 ('I sent before you Moses, Aaron, and Miriam'); Psalm 105:26.
historicalTrivia: The verb *shalach* ('I will send you') makes Moses the premier 'Sent One' (*Shaliach* / Apostle) of the Old Testament!

dominicalIntent: But Moses said to God: 'Who am I that I should go to Pharaoh and bring the children of Israel out of Egypt?' (*Mi anochi ki elekh el-Par'oh...*). FIRST OBJECTION: 'WHO AM I?!' Moses responds in profound humility and self-doubt: **'WHO AM I THAT I SHOULD GO TO PHARAOH?'**
cccReferences: CCC 2575 (Moses' humility before the magnitude of the divine call); Exod 4:10.
historicalContext: Humility of the 80-year-old desert shepherd.
translationNuances: Hebrew *Vayyo'mer Moshe el-ha-Elohim Mi anochi ki elekh el-Par'oh ve-khi otzi eth-bney Yisra'el mi-Mitzrayim*: *Mi anochi* ('Who am I?').
crossReferences: Exodus 4:10; 1 Samuel 18:18; 2 Samuel 7:18 ('Who am I, O Lord God?'); Jeremiah 1:6.
historicalTrivia: Profound contrast: 40 years earlier Moses thought he could deliver Israel by force (Exod 2:12); after 40 years in the desert, he realizes his total nothingness without God!

dominicalIntent: He said: 'But I will be with you, and this shall be the sign for you, that I have sent you: when you have brought the people out of Egypt, you shall serve God on this mountain' (*Ki-ehyeh immakh... ta'avdun eth-ha-Elohim al ha-har ha-zeh*). 'I WILL BE WITH YOU!' AND THE SIGN OF MOUNT SINAI! God promises: (1) **'I WILL BE WITH YOU!' (*Ki-ehyeh immakh*)**, (2) **The Sign**: 'When you bring the people out of Egypt, **YOU SHALL WORSHIP GOD ON THIS VERY MOUNTAIN (SINAI)!'**
cccReferences: CCC 2575 (Divine accompaniment guaranteeing the mission); CCC 2063; Josh 1:5; Matt 28:20.
historicalContext: Promise of divine presence (*Emmanuel*) and future worship covenant at Sinai.
translationNuances: Hebrew *Vayyo'mer ki-ehyeh immakh ve-zeh-lekha ha-oth ki anochi shelachtikha be-hotzi'akha eth-ha-am mi-Mitzrayim ta'avdun eth-ha-Elohim al ha-har ha-zeh*: *Ki-ehyeh immakh* ('For I will be with you'). *ta'avdun* ('you shall serve/worship').
crossReferences: Joshua 1:5; Matthew 28:20 ('I am with you always'); Exodus 19:1-3; Acts 7:7.
historicalTrivia: The promise *Ki-ehyeh immakh* ('I will be with you') uses the exact verb *Ehyeh* ('I AM') revealed in verse 14!

dominicalIntent: Then Moses said to God: 'If I come to the people of Israel and say to them, "The God of your fathers has sent me to you," and they ask me, "What is his name?" what shall I say to them?' SECOND OBJECTION: 'WHAT IS HIS NAME?' Moses asks for the essential Name of God.
cccReferences: CCC 203 (The revelation of the Divine Name as the foundation of prayer and covenant); CCC 2575.
historicalContext: In ancient Near Eastern culture, knowing a god's personal Name expressed true knowledge of his nature.
translationNuances: Hebrew *Vayyo'mer Moshe el-ha-Elohim hinneh anochi va el-bney Yisra'el ve-amarthi lahem Elohey avotheykhem shlachani alehkhem ve-amru-li mah-shemo mah omar alehem*: *mah-shemo* ('What is His Name?').
historicalTrivia: In ancient Egypt, gods had secret names (*rn*); Moses asks for Yahweh's true Name.

dominicalIntent: God said to Moses: 'I AM WHO I AM.' And he said: 'Say this to the people of Israel: "I AM has sent me to you."' (*EHYEH ASHER EHYEH... Ehyeh shlachani alehkhem*). THE SUPREME REVELATION OF THE DIVINE NAME: I AM WHO I AM (*EHYEH ASHER EHYEH*)! **THE MOST IMPORTANT THEOLOGICAL VERSE IN ALL OF SACRED SCRIPTURE!** God reveals His Name: **EHYEH ASHER EHYEH** ('I AM WHO I AM' / 'I AM BEING ITSELF'!). **GOD IS THE UNCASED, SELF-EXISTENT, ETERNAL, TRANSFORMATIONLESS BEING ITSELF (*IPSUM ESSE SUBSISTENS*)! JESUS CHRIST CLAIMS THIS EXACT DIVINE NAME IN JOHN 8:58: 'BEFORE ABRAHAM WAS, I AM (*EGO EIMI*)!'**
cccReferences: CCC 203-213 (THE REVELATION OF THE DIVINE NAME: God is Being itself, eternal, unchangeable, faithful, and pure love); CCC 206 ('In revealing his mysterious name YHWH, God says who he is and by what name he is to be called'); CCC 213; CCC 2575; John 8:58 ('Before Abraham was, I AM'); John 18:5-6.
historicalContext: The supreme divine self-revelation at the Burning Bush.
translationNuances: Hebrew *Vayyo'mer Elohim el-Moshe EHYEH ASHER EHYEH vayyo'mer koh thomar li-vney Yisra'el EHYEH shlachani alehkhem*: *EHYEH ASHER EHYEH* ('I AM WHO I AM' / 'I WILL BE WHAT I WILL BE', LXX *Egō eimi ho ōn* = 'I am the Existing One' -> St. Thomas Aquinas *Ipsum Esse Subsistens*!). *EHYEH* ('I AM').
crossReferences: John 8:58; John 18:5-6; Revelation 1:8 ('Who is and who was and who is to come'); Exodus 6:3; Isaiah 43:10.
historicalTrivia: St. Thomas Aquinas (*Summa Theologiae* I, q. 13, a. 11) proved that *I AM WHO I AM* (*He-Who-Is*) is the most proper Name of God, because it signifies Being Itself without limit or determination!

dominicalIntent: God also said to Moses: 'Say this to the people of Israel: "The Lord, the God of your fathers, the God of Abraham, the God of Isaac, and the God of Jacob, has sent me to you." This is my name forever, and thus I am to be remembered throughout all generations' (*YHVH Elohey avotheykhem... zeh-shemi le-olam ve-zeh zikhri le-dor dor*). THE TETRAGRAMMATON (**YHWH**) REVEALED AS HIS NAME FOREVER!
